```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(risk.decision)
```

This illustrative project-selection example compares two alternatives using
explicit probability-consequence pairs, in the spirit of quantitative risk
analysis rather than ordinal likelihood and impact scores. It is not a
reproduction or implementation of Hubbard's proprietary spreadsheet. The
invented figures are not from his book.

Frame: choose one project. Uncertainty: demand is low or high. The outcomes
are net benefits in arbitrary monetary units, with larger numbers preferred.
Each alternative has its own conditional probability distribution.

```{r}
path <- system.file("extdata", "project_selection.csv", package = "risk.decision")
projects <- import_risk_data(path)
projects
calculate_expected_value(projects)
calculate_risk_metrics(projects, threshold = 0)
```

```{r}
generate_risk_matrix(projects, ylab = "Net benefit (arbitrary units)")
plot_risk_visualization(projects, ylab = "Expected net benefit")
```

These plots preserve meaningful numerical inputs instead of combining ordinal
categories. Expected net benefit is not a complete preference model: compare
the chance of loss, distribution shape and decision maker's risk attitude
before choosing. Coincident points may overlap in the first plot.
